asian-stir-fry-vegetables-cooked-fat-add.title: Asian Stir Fry Vegetables, Cooked, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: Asian stir‑fry vegetables are a blend of sliced vegetables (broccoli, carrots, bell peppers, snap peas, mushrooms, etc.) that have been lightly sautéed in a small amount of oil. The product is ready to eat – simply reheat in a wok or microwave.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix often includes vegetables typical for Asian cuisine such as bamboo shoots and water chestnuts.
Vegetables cook quickly – usually 3‑5 minutes over high heat.
Adding a modest amount of fat enhances flavor and aids absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
The product is commonly used in wok and street‑food dishes in fast‑casual restaurants.
Formulations are often gluten‑free and contain no added sugar.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The vegetables provide vitamin B6 and folate, which support metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Broccoli and bell peppers are high in vitamin C and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes healthy bowel movements and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: When the added oil is kept moderate, a serving contains few calories, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Improves nutrient absorption
items.content: A small amount of fat helps the body better absorb fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.

items.title: Allergy to specific vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may react to soy sauce, sesame, or other ingredients sometimes included in the blend.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain versions may contain added soy sauce, increasing the salt level.

items.title: Excess fat intake
items.content: Using too much added oil can raise the calorie count and strain the digestive system.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the vegetables over high heat for 3‑5 minutes, optionally adding soy sauce, ginger, or garlic. Serve as a side dish, over rice or noodles, or as the main component of a wok‑style stir‑fry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in the original packaging or an airtight container for up to 5 days. After opening, use within 2‑3 days for best quality.

green-peas-canned-reduced-sodium-cooked-.title: Green peas, canned, reduced sodium, cooked, fat added, NS as to fat type

content.title: About
content.content: Canned green peas are a ready‑to‑eat product made from fresh pea pods that are blanched, drained, and sealed in a reduced‑sodium brine. A vegetable oil is added, but the specific type of fat is not specified (NS). The peas retain their bright green color, natural sweetness, and a slight snap when eaten.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peas are a good source of plant protein and dietary fiber.
Canning extends shelf life to 2–3 years while preserving most nutrients.
Reduced‑sodium brine makes the product suitable for low‑salt diets.
Added fat enhances flavor and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Peas belong to the legume family, along with beans, lentils, and soy.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of canned peas provides about 8 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps regulate blood glucose levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas contain vitamin B6, thiamine, and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium, and phosphorus in peas support blood health and bone strength.

items.title: Reduced sodium content
items.content: Lower salt levels make the product more suitable for people monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Added fat increases calories
items.content: The oil raises the caloric density, so portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Sodium still present
items.content: Even reduced, the product contains salt, which can be an issue for hypertension.

items.title: Possible fermentation after opening
items.content: Once opened, store the can in the refrigerator and consume within 3–4 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peas can be eaten cold in salads, added to soups, stews, or pasta dishes. They also heat quickly in the microwave or on the stovetop with a splash of water or broth. Season with herbs, spices, or a squeeze of lemon for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer leftovers to an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 4 days. Discard if an off‑odor or discoloration develops.

pretzels-hard-peanut-butter-filled.title: Hard Pretzels with Peanut Butter Filling

content.title: About
content.content: Hard pretzels with a peanut butter filling are salty, knot‑shaped baked snacks with a crisp outer crust and a smooth, slightly sweet peanut butter center. They combine the crunch of traditional pretzel dough with the richness of roasted peanuts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Classic German pretzels are made from a simple dough, but modern versions often add flavorings and fillings.
The peanut butter filling is usually made from roasted peanuts, salt, and a touch of sugar.
The crisp crust is achieved by a double‑baking process: the dough is first boiled in a lye solution, then baked until golden.
Pretzels are commonly served with beer, but they also make a quick energy snack in school lunchboxes.
In the United States, over 200 million packages of flavored pretzels are sold each year.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides about 25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats in peanuts promote heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Peanut butter supplies iron, essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Sustains energy
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from the dough and fats from the peanut butter offers lasting satiety.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: These pretzels can trigger severe allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to peanuts.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The salty crust may be unsuitable for people with hypertension; low‑salt versions are recommended.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Because of the fats in the filling and carbs in the dough, the snack is relatively high in calories; portion control is advised.

items.title: Choking hazard for young children
items.content: The hard texture can pose a choking risk for small kids; offer broken pieces or smaller portions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy pretzels straight from the bag, crumble them into salads, use as a base for appetizers, or dip them in cheese or yogurt sauces. They can also be broken and drizzled with chocolate for a sweet twist.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation. Discard if you notice a rancid smell or texture changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Pumpkin seeds are the edible kernels of pumpkin (Cucurbita pepo) that are traditionally enjoyed as a salted snack. They have a mild nutty flavor with a pronounced salty note and a crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pumpkin seeds are rich in magnesium, iron, and zinc.
Ancient cultures used them as a portable source of energy for travel and hunting.
They are one of the few plant sources of heart‑healthy triglycerides.
In the United States more than 1 billion pounds of pumpkin seeds are produced each year.
Salted seeds are a popular bar snack and often served with beer.

items.title: Rich in magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle, nerve, and cardiovascular function.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is essential for immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Pumpkin seeds provide vitamin E and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports prostate health
items.content: Research suggests that zinc and phytosterols in the seeds may benefit prostate function.

items.title: Provides plant protein
items.content: One cup of seeds delivers about 30 g of protein, making them a valuable source for vegetarians.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pumpkin seeds.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salted varieties can contribute to elevated blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Seeds are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Additives
items.content: Commercial products may contain artificial flavorings and preservatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Seeds can be eaten straight as a snack, added to salads, yogurt, granola, baked goods, or used as a topping for soups. They are often roasted and salted before consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.

rice-white-with-soy-based-sauce-fat-adde.title: White Rice with Soy Sauce and Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: White rice cooked with soy sauce and a touch of vegetable fat is a fragrant dish with a soft texture and a rich, savory flavor. Rice provides a primary source of carbohydrates, while soy sauce adds salty‑umami notes and the fat makes the meal more satisfying.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is one of the most widely consumed grains worldwide.
Soy sauce was invented in China over 2,000 years ago as a method of preserving food.
Adding a small amount of fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins from soy sauce.
Rice with soy sauce is a staple side dish in many Asian cuisines, often served alongside meat or fish.
Properly stored cooked rice can keep in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of energy thanks to its high content of complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Rich in glucose
items.content: Glucose from rice is rapidly available to the bloodstream, supporting blood‑sugar levels and brain function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Soy sauce contributes a modest amount of iron, which is essential for blood formation.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Rice is easy to digest, and the added fat helps with the absorption of other nutrients.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Soy sauce contains phenolic compounds that have antioxidant properties.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, which may be problematic for people with diabetes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce is high in sodium; excessive intake can contribute to elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy sauce.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The added fat increases the calorie count, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice with soy sauce and fat as a side dish with meat, fish, or vegetables, use it in sushi rolls, fried rice, or as a quick microwave meal. Garnish with sliced green onions or toasted sesame seeds for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 4 days. Reheat to steaming temperature before serving. Discard rice that has been left at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
